title: Three groups, one rail
desc: How the Compliance Center is laid out, and where a question goes.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can find any compliance question's home in the rail, read a row's status without opening it, and tell what the Calendar and Reports tabs are for.

steps.title: Frameworks, Registers, Admin
steps.bodyMd:
The Compliance Center is one rail with three headings, and the headings are the whole mental model.

- **Frameworks** are the things that score you. GDPR, AI Act and ISO 27001 are always there; the rest appear once your organisation switches them on.
- **Registers** are the things you keep. Requests, incidents, the processing register, risks, policies, audits.
- **Admin** is the plumbing: Settings, and Evidence connectors.

A framework asks *are we compliant*. A register is *the book you write in*. They are not layers of each other.

steps.title: A register is not under a framework
steps.bodyMd:
This is the part people get wrong. A register does not belong to one regulation.

Record one breach at Van Dijk Groep and that single incident counts for **GDPR Art. 33**, for **ISO 27001 A.5.24**, and — if the organisation has the CRA switched on — for its reporting duty too. One row, three obligations.

That is why Registers is its own group and not a sub-list under ISO 27001. If you go looking for the Risk register *inside* ISO, you will not find it.

steps.question: Van Dijk Groep records one suspected data breach. Which of these does that single row feed?

choices.label: Only whichever framework page you were on when you recorded it
choices.feedback: The register is not scoped to the page you came from. The row exists once and every framework that cares about incidents reads it.

choices.label: Nothing, until an auditor asks for it
choices.feedback: The clock starts at detection whether or not anyone asks. That is the reason Incidents is a register and not a form you fill in later.

steps.explanation: Registers serve several frameworks at once. One incident row is simultaneously GDPR evidence, an ISO control record, and — where the CRA is enabled — a reporting obligation.

steps.title: The number on the right is the answer
steps.bodyMd:
Every rail row carries its own status on the right, so you can triage without opening anything:

- **Requests (DSR)** — an overdue badge and `{n} open`
- **Incidents & breaches** — a clock, the hours left, and `{n} open`
- **Risk register** — `{n} · {high} high`
- **SoA (Annex A)** — `{approved}/{total} approved`
- **Policies** — `{n} · {due} review`
- **Training & competence** — `{done}/{total}`

A number that the server did not send renders as nothing at all. A blank is not a zero — it means *not known*, and the product refuses to invent the difference.

steps.title: Read the rail without opening it
steps.instruction: Match each thing you see on a row to the question it answers.

pairs.left: A clock and "14 h" on Incidents & breaches
pairs.right: How long until the Art. 33 deadline
pairs.note: The incident row counts down from detection, not from when you opened the page.

pairs.right: How much of the Statement of Applicability is decided
pairs.note: 93 is the full Annex A control set; approved is the last rung of the decision ladder.

pairs.left: A blank where a number should be
pairs.right: The server could not answer — not "zero"
pairs.note: Rendering a 0 the server never sent would be a lie an auditor could act on.

pairs.left: "Evidence chain intact · SHA-256" in the footer
pairs.right: The ledger has not been tampered with
pairs.note: If it ever reads "Evidence chain broken", the integrity report is the next stop.

steps.title: Two ways to cut the rail down
steps.bodyMd:
At the top of the rail sit the only two controls you need on a busy morning.

**All / Needs attention** is a two-way switch. Needs attention carries a badge with the count, and hides every row that has nothing wrong with it.

**Search** takes more than section names — the placeholder says *Search checks, articles or registers…* and it means it. Type an article number and you land on the check that scores it. Nothing found reads *Nothing matches*.

steps.question: You want the check behind GDPR Art. 32. What is the shortest route?

choices.label: Type the article number into the rail's search box
Open GDPR, then read down the Checks table until you see it
choices.feedback: That works, but search covers checks, articles and registers precisely so you do not have to scan a table.

choices.label: Switch the rail to Needs attention
choices.feedback: Needs attention filters by what is failing, not by article — a passing Art. 32 check would vanish from the list.

steps.explanation: The search box is indexed over checks, article numbers and register names, which makes it the fastest path to a specific obligation.

steps.title: Overview → Status
steps.bodyMd:
The Overview opens on **Status**: the **Overall score** ring, and under it four counters — **Passing**, **Warnings**, **Failing**, **Not applicable**.

The subtitle tells you what to do with them: *Fix the red items first.*

Underneath, the **Needs attention** card lists work in the order that matters — failing first, then by severity. When there is genuinely nothing, it says so plainly: *Nothing needs attention — every check passes or is not applicable.*

steps.title: Run now, and why it is sometimes greyed out
steps.bodyMd:
The header carries **Run now** as its primary button. While a sweep runs the label becomes *Running…*.

Before onboarding is finished the button is disabled and its tooltip says **Available after setup** — a score computed before the organisation has told the product who its DPO is and which legal bases it relies on would be a number about nothing.

Beside it, a chip reads `Last run {time} · every {hours} h`. Checks sweep on their own schedule; **Run now** is for when you have just changed something and want the score to catch up.

steps.title: Overview → Calendar
steps.bodyMd:
The second tab is the one nobody expects and everybody needs: every clock the organisation is running, on one page.

It collects the deadlines that already exist elsewhere — a data-subject request's 30 days, an incident's 72 hours, a CRA early warning and its full report, an obligation you scheduled, an attestation about to expire — and shows each as a bar with how far through it you are.

Nothing is authored here. The Calendar is a view over work that already exists in the registers.

steps.title: Overview → Reports
steps.bodyMd:
The third tab is where the documents live, and it is also where the ISO readiness numbers moved to.

It is the one place to fetch the **Statement of Applicability**, **Clause conformity**, the **Risk register**, the **Policy pack** and the **Full evidence bundle** — the Stage-1 document set a certification body asks for.

The rail has a shortcut to it too: the small reports button at the top, labelled *Reports and downloads* for screen readers.

steps.title: Monday morning, in order
steps.instruction: Marieke opens the Compliance Center and has twenty minutes. Put her steps in the order that gets the most risk off the table.

items.label: Switch the rail to Needs attention
Deal with the incident counting down in hours
Deal with the data-subject request counting down in days
Work the Needs attention card, failing items first
Press Run now so the score reflects the fixes

sim.feedback: Filter first so the rail only shows work. Then the shortest clock wins: a breach deadline is measured in hours and a request in days. Failing checks come after the statutory clocks, and re-running the sweep is last — it reports on what you did, it does not do anything.

steps.title: Your turn: route four questions
steps.instruction: Van Dijk Groep's account manager forwards you four things in one morning. Say which rail row you open for each, and why. (1) A customer asks whether you have a signed processing agreement with your American transcription supplier. (2) An engineer reports he mailed a parts list to the wrong address. (3) A prospect's security questionnaire asks which Annex A controls you have excluded and why. (4) A colleague asks whether she still has to acknowledge the new acceptable-use policy.
steps.placeholder: 1) Processing register (ROPA) — the processors table records each operator, its location and whether an SCC is attested…

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- Route any compliance question to the right rail row, because you know a framework **scores** and a register **records**.
- Triage from the rail alone: the meta on each row is the status, and a blank is *unknown*, never zero.
- Use the Overview's three tabs for three different jobs — Status to fix, Calendar to see what is due, Reports to hand something to an auditor.

ex-compliance-center-map-where.title: Route four questions to their register
ex-compliance-center-map-where.task: Name the rail row for four incoming compliance questions and justify each choice.
criteria: Question 1 goes to Processing register (ROPA) — specifically its processors table, where an operator's location and SCC/DPA state are recorded
Question 2 goes to Incidents & breaches, and the answer recognises that recording starts the 72-hour clock immediately
Question 3 goes to SoA (Annex A), and mentions that an excluded control still needs a written justification
Question 4 goes to Policies (acknowledgements) or Training & competence, and does not confuse either with the Learning Center's own courses
ex-compliance-center-map-where.guidance: Do not pass an answer that files the misdirected e-mail under Requests (DSR) — a data-subject request is someone exercising their rights, not a mistake the organisation made. Do not pass an answer that puts the Annex A question under ISO 27001's framework page: the framework page scores controls, the SoA records the decisions. An answer that names the right row but gives no reason is at most a borderline pass; the reasoning is the thing being taught.

practiceTopic.title: Finding your way around the Compliance Center
practiceTopic.summary: The rail's three groups, what each row's meta means, and the Overview's three tabs.
facts: The rail groups rows under three headings: Frameworks, Registers and Admin.
Registers serve several frameworks at once — one incident row counts for GDPR Art. 33, ISO 27001 A.5.24 and the CRA reporting duty.
The rail's segmented control switches between All and Needs attention, and Needs attention carries the attention count as a badge.
The rail search placeholder is "Search checks, articles or registers…" and an empty result reads "Nothing matches".
The Overview has three tabs: Status, Calendar and Reports.
Run now is disabled until onboarding is finished, and its tooltip then reads "Available after setup".
The rail footer reads "Evidence chain intact · {rows} rows · SHA-256", or "Evidence chain broken — check the integrity report".
A number the server did not send renders as nothing at all — a blank means unknown, not zero.
